metadata.description: 8 documented ecological cascade narratives showing how species decline ripples through the web

cascades.title: The Sand Eel Collapse
cascades.subtitle: How warming seas starve seabird colonies across the North Sea
cascades.trigger: Climate warming shifts plankton communities northward, reducing sand eel food base. Industrial fishing compounds decline.

steps.event: Sand eel populations decline as warming North Sea shifts cold-water plankton northward. Industrial fishing historically removed ~1 million tonnes per year.
Puffin chicks starve in burrows as parents cannot find enough sand eels. One in four UK puffins lost since 2000. BTO projects potential 90% decline by 2050.
Seals switch from sand eels to gadid fish, buffering their population but increasing pressure on commercial fisheries.
Salmon condition and survival at sea reduced as sand eel prey declines during marine phase.

cascades.resolution: UK banned industrial sand eel fishing in March 2024. An earlier 20,000km² closure off Scotland's east coast produced measurable improvement in kittiwake breeding success.

cascades.title: The Mink Invasion
cascades.subtitle: Fur farm escapees triggered Britain's fastest mammal decline — now otters are fighting back
cascades.trigger: American mink escaped and were released from fur farms throughout the 20th century, establishing wild populations across nearly all of Britain.

steps.event: Feral mink populations establish across Britain. Female mink are small enough to enter water vole burrows and kill mothers with pups.
Fastest mammal decline in British history: 94% loss. From ~8 million to fewer than 186,000. Riparian habitat simplifies without vole grazing and burrowing.
Mink predate bank-nesting kingfishers, suppressing nesting success along affected waterways.
Otter recovery displaces mink — mink occupancy drops from 77% to 23% within one year. Otters are too large for vole burrows, restoring natural predator-prey balance.
Reduced mink predation benefits amphibian populations along rivers where otters have returned.

cascades.resolution: Otter recovery is naturally suppressing mink. Dedicated mink eradication programmes (Waterlife Recovery Trust) have produced documented water vole recovery at target sites.
keySources: Rushton et al. (2000) Journal of Applied Ecology 37:475–490

cascades.title: Grey Squirrel Invasion
cascades.subtitle: An invasive species unravelling woodland across two centuries
cascades.trigger: Grey squirrels introduced from North America between 1876 and 1929. Now 2.7 million vs 287,000 reds.

steps.event: Greys outcompete reds for acorns (superior tannin digestion) and carry squirrelpox virus (~100% fatal to reds, harmless to greys).
Population crashes 92%. Confined to Scotland, parts of northern England, and isolated island populations. Squirrelpox accelerates replacement 20× faster.
Grey squirrels strip bark from young trees (10–40 years), causing £37M annual damage. Threatens the next generation of mature oaks that support 2,300+ species.
Jay-oak mutualism persists but reduced acorn availability due to grey squirrel consumption before ripening may affect jay populations long-term.

cascades.resolution: UK Squirrel Accord coordinates grey squirrel management. Fertility control research (immunocontraception) offers a humane long-term solution. Pine marten recovery in Scotland naturally suppresses grey squirrels.
keySources: Gurnell et al. (2004) Journal of Animal Ecology 73:26–35
Tompkins et al. (2002) Proc. R. Soc. B 269:529–533

cascades.title: The Badger-Hedgehog Triangle
cascades.subtitle: Intraguild predation, competition, and a crumbling food foundation
cascades.trigger: Agricultural intensification reduces hedgehog habitat while badger populations double. Earthworm decline adds bottom-up pressure.

steps.event: 33–41% decline over 25 years from agricultural intensification. Foundation food source for both badgers and hedgehogs.
Population doubled to ~562,000. Both predates hedgehogs (only UK animal that can overcome spines) and competes for invertebrate food (consuming ~5× more per individual).
From ~30 million in the 1950s to fewer than 900,000. Experimental badger removal doubled hedgehog counts. Hedgehog decline reduces slug/snail predation.
Frogs face cumulative predation pressure from both badgers and foxes; hedgehog decline removes one minor predator of frog eggs but does not compensate.

cascades.resolution: Hedgehog Street campaign promotes garden connectivity (hedgehog highways). Creating invertebrate-rich habitat benefits both hedgehogs and badgers by reducing competition.

cascades.title: The Invisible Foundation
cascades.subtitle: Earthworm decline ripples through the entire web
cascades.trigger: Agricultural intensification, soil compaction, and chemical use drive 33–41% earthworm decline over 25 years.

steps.event: First century-scale UK meta-analysis reveals 33–41% decline. 42% of UK farmland may lack key earthworm functional groups. Contributes 6.5% of global grain production.
Reduced soil engineering degrades conditions beneath oaks: poorer drainage, slower nutrient cycling, weaker growth.
80% of diet is earthworms. Decline forces dietary shifts and may increase predation on hedgehogs and other prey.
Major food source declining, compounding habitat loss and badger competition pressures.
Invertebrate prey decline in farmland reduces chick-rearing food availability.
Earthworms are a wet-weather supplementary food. Their decline narrows dietary options when primary prey is scarce.
Reduced soil nutrient cycling affects woodland wildflower growth. Earthworms boost plant production by 25% on average.

cascades.resolution: Regenerative farming practices (no-till, cover crops, reduced chemical inputs) can rebuild earthworm populations. UK government's Environmental Land Management scheme incentivises soil health.
keySources: Barnes et al. (2023) PLOS ONE PMC10069791
Van Groenigen et al. (2014) Scientific Reports 4:6365
Blouin et al. (2013) European Journal of Soil Science 64:161–182

cascades.title: The Salmon Artery
cascades.subtitle: When the nutrient pipeline between ocean and upland breaks
cascades.trigger: Salmon classified Endangered in GB (2023). 63% decline over three generations from warming seas, river barriers, pollution, and sea lice from fish farms.

steps.event: 63% decline severs the marine-to-freshwater nutrient pipeline. 2,000-year sediment records show salmon historically delivered marine nitrogen and phosphorus to rivers.
Riparian earthworm populations lose marine nutrient subsidies from salmon carcasses, reducing soil invertebrate productivity.
With fewer salmon, otters shift to crayfish (14% of summer diet in chalk streams), frogs, and waterbirds.
Fewer salmon parr and fry in shallow riffles reduces one prey source for kingfishers.
Increased otter predation on remaining native crayfish populations. Signal crayfish invasion compounds pressure.

cascades.resolution: River barrier removal, fish passage installation, and wild salmon recovery programmes. Atlantic Salmon Trust's Likely Suspects Framework tracks marine survival factors.
keySources: Bernthal et al. (2022) Aquatic Conservation PMC9314074
Woodward et al. (2021) Frontiers in Ecology & Evolution 9:675261

cascades.title: The Pollinator Spiral
cascades.subtitle: A self-reinforcing decline between flowers and their pollinators
cascades.trigger: Agricultural intensification removes wildflower habitat. 25% average range shrinkage for British bee and hoverfly species since 1980.

steps.event: 50% of UK hedgerows lost since 1945. Removes early-season nectar for emerging bumblebee queens and nesting habitat.
Generalist species remains stable, masking collapse of specialist pollinators. One-third of British bee species declining. Two bumblebee species extinct.
Only 25% of UK peatlands in good condition. Loss removes medicinal nectar that protects bumblebees from gut parasites.
86% decline since 1976 in a formerly 'common' butterfly. Demonstrates that even generalists can crash when food web simplifies.
60% decline partly driven by aerial insect loss. Pollinators and other insects form the shared food web supporting insectivorous birds.

cascades.resolution: National Pollinator Strategy; agri-environment schemes paying farmers for wildflower margins; urban pollinator corridors. Just four plant species now account for half of Britain's nectar — diversification is critical.
keySources: Koch et al. Current Biology (Kew heather-bumblebee)

cascades.title: The Hen Harrier Conflict
cascades.subtitle: Where ecology collides with economics on Britain's moors
cascades.trigger: Grouse shooting generates significant economic value from managed moorland. Hen harrier predation on grouse chicks threatens this revenue.

steps.event: Rotational burning for grouse management creates a mosaic of young and old heather — the habitat structure both grouse and harriers depend on.
Britain's only endemic bird subspecies. ~90% of diet is heather shoots. Population managed for driven shooting.
Predation on grouse chicks can make shooting unviable at high harrier density. England could support 300+ pairs but only 4–12 nesting attempts occur due to illegal persecution.
Fox control on grouse moors reduces predation on ground-nesting birds. This inadvertently benefits skylarks and waders on adjacent farmland.

cascades.resolution: RSPB Hen Harrier LIFE project; satellite tagging exposes illegal killing; diversionary feeding trials show harrier predation can be managed without persecution.
keySources: Thirgood & Redpath (2008) Journal of Applied Ecology 45:982–991
Hudson & Newborn (1995) Manual of Red Grouse
